title: Climate and Spiritual Activism
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up how Zen practice informs spiritual activism on climate, working through Dogen's fascicle Valley Sounds and Mountain Colors and Layman Dong Po's verse about the valley's long, broad tongue. Reizan reads Daido Loori on understanding self and universe together, tells of a Maasai junior elder in a National Geographic story who says trees grow in families, and reads "The Tent," an old poem in which ravens and bulldozers blur into a waking dream. Dongshan's five ranks lead from separation toward a compassion that puts one's life on the line. Reizan ends with the Lorax, who speaks for the trees as one of them.

sentences.text: Hi everyone.
I think, I don't know, this might be just my first time practicing in person with other people in forever.
It does feel nice.
It feels really different.
I feel like we said so much in the service, I wonder what I could add to all of that.
But of course, I've got more words to add.
Can everyone here online hear?
Well, no good.
We've got Bob Andrews and Ken and John Wiley and Scott, and Travis is here, and somebody else dialing in from a phone number.
And here in the room, we've got Terrell and Karen McNeans and Chris Burkhart and Kate and myself.
Oh, it looks like Wayne showed up here too.
Great.
A couple of little announcements.
One is that this is the first of this month of doing senior student talks.
We did this in July: Tim usually takes a sabbatical in July and tries to get some time off, so senior students fill in.
There was a suggestion in the practice committee that maybe this period of time between the Rohatsu and practice period is another opportunity for something like that.
So we've got another little round of several talks coming up over the next few weeks.
One of them, I believe, will be a Sunday talk.
Look for those; they were mentioned in the newsletter that came out recently.
Another little piece of news: I've been the Eno for the last couple of years now, the pandemic Eno, I guess, is what it's been.
It's been interesting for me, because it worked in terms of what was going on with me, which is that my body kind of fell apart in the same time trajectory as COVID.
When we had to stop working, I had to stop working.
My ability to sit is still barely there.
I wasn't able to sit the whole period today.
But obviously, on Zoom, I've been able to manage working that out.
We generally try to do a job like this for a couple of years, so it's my time to rotate out, and we're getting back to in-person things, which I'm having a harder time doing physically.
So this month, Chris Burkhart is going to start filling in officially as Eno.
I also want to acknowledge Kate McKenna, who has been acting as essentially assistant Eno and filling in as Eno at many times throughout the year.
Great thanks to everyone for this opportunity.
I've really enjoyed it, serving the community.
It has helped me be engaged with everyone.
And I hope that, and we made it through a difficult period of time, and now we're able at least to see each other a little bit.
So we'll keep hoping and looking forward to how the pandemic unfolds with our practice schedule.
We're going to keep attention to how we need to shift and change it as we go along.
A couple of weeks ago, we had a Sangha conversation meeting and we hosted Julie Johnson from the Multifaith Network for Climate Justice, which I've been representing our group with.

It's a multifaith group in the local community, different churches and denominations and organizations, all dedicated to seeing how we can engage, from our spiritual and religious viewpoints, as activists in climate change justice.
We had an interesting discussion there.
If you missed that conversation, the last newsletter that went out has a link to the meeting notes, so you can find out some of what was said during that discussion.
The climate issue that we're all dealing with is huge.
It's the issue of our age.
We do get sidetracked by thinking about many other things, but meanwhile, this continues, and we have to find how to respond as humans, and particularly as practitioners.
So the question posed during that meeting was: how does your practice inform what you consider to be a life of spiritual activism?
Perhaps we imagine that our endeavor towards enlightenment is the saving grace for all beings, and that our work, as we are working on our cushion, is enough.
And certainly it is, and it is the heart of any spiritual activism: engagement with our practice.

Our obvious concern, I think, when we think about a life dedicated to activism, is a worry that we may get involved in trying to change things outside ourselves, and that might just get muddled up with grasping and aversion and pull us away from a centeredness in our own practice.
So that's the worry as we try to engage in the world and activity, right?
Obviously that is not what we want to engage in with activism.
So how do we answer this question?

In looking into this, I thought going into the heart of some things about our Soto way, our tradition, can give us some inspiration and some teachings to help balance our personal efforts to practice with this life dedicated to relieving the suffering of all beings.

Roshi John Daido Loori, who has passed away now, but was the leader of Zen Mountain Monastery, Mount Tremper in New York, has a beautiful little book, a tiny little book called Teachings of the Insentient, which is about how we learn from inanimate nature, what it has to teach us.
He said a little bit in here about threading the needle of this effort.
*How we understand the self is how we understand the universe, and how we understand the universe determines how we relate to it and how we combust our lives within it.*
I like that use of the word "combust," to combust our lives within it, to use ourselves up in the effort of living.
It's to understand ourselves by understanding the universe, and understanding the universe by understanding ourselves.
This sounds very much like a line from Dogen.
So we can see the relationship right there in the teachings of our practice about how to begin to look at and relate to the world in this effort.
I'd do a little mash-up here between this idea and one of Dogen's fascicles, Valley Sounds and Mountain Colors.
At the very opening of this fascicle, Dogen talks about this idea of combusting yourself, but differently, perhaps something about slipping out of your skin.
*Slipping out of your old skin, not constrained by past views, you manifest immediately what has been dormant for boundless eons.
As this very moment manifests, "I" don't know, "who" doesn't know, you have no expectations, and the "Buddha I" sees beyond seeing.
This experience is beyond the realm of human thinking.*
Dogen wrote this fascicle in 1240, and this was a very fruitful year for him.
He wrote many fascicles this year that are well known now, such as Uji, The Time Being, and The Mountains and Waters Sutra, and Power of the Robe, all in very short order.
So it was a very fertile time for him in thinking through the practice.

He begins this fascicle on this idea of the permeability of our sense of self, slipping out of your old skin, and goes on to put quotation marks around the words, or at least, 'cause Tanahashi did, who translated, so I suppose there's some reason for that.
Quotation marks around the words "I," "who," "you," and "the Buddha I."
All these are presented as singular points of view, parts of what he says in the end is simply human thinking.
In other words, conceptualization caught in a dualistic outcome.
He offers all this by way of introducing the story of one who has slipped out of his old skin, Layman Dong Po.
This is a ninth century practitioner, contemporary with Zhaozhou.
He was camping out one night in a valley on the slopes of Mount Lu, and he composed this verse.
*Valley sounds are the long, broad tongue.
Mountain colors are no other than the unconditioned body.
Eighty-four thousand verses are heard through the night.
What can I say about this in the morning?*

And [unclear: "proved Zhaozhou"], of course, had always emphasized the idea of sentient or insentient strongly in his teachings, such as when he confounded any assumption of the possession of Buddha nature by a dog.
Or when asked once, "What is the essential meaning of the Buddha Dharma?" he replied, "The cypress tree at the front of the courtyard."
Because how could the essential meaning of the Buddha Dharma be any more complex and miraculous, or really be anything apart from the cypress tree in the courtyard?
We can think of some other old teachings about sentient or insentient, such as that old story of the Zen teacher and a student rapping on the casket: alive or dead?
The teacher says, "I won't say.
I won't say."
What is the earth saying to us?
What are we saying to the earth?
I sometimes come to these Dharma talks not knowing anything about what to say.
And I find, interestingly, that I pull up materials that seem at hand, and everything speaks to the Dharma.
So last night in the grocery aisle, I picked up a National Geographic and brought it home.

Instead of talking about how trees communicate with each other from some newfangled scientific understanding, I found this story from the Loita forest of the Maasai tribe, far above the Serengeti plains, in a hidden rainforest where the author was permitted to go by just some personal connections he had, to meet the old man who was the descended spiritual advisor to the tribe and protector of the forest, to see if he would be allowed admittance.
And he was, and he went on a ten-mile hike the next day with a junior elder, Langatut Olay Kuya.
At one point they stopped in a grove and Langatut said:
*Trees grow in families.
Older trees nurture and guide young trees.
They share friendships among themselves and with people.*
Upon getting back that day, the old elder asked him, "What did you see?"
And he said, "I saw my ignorance."
And the elder said, "What else did you see?"
In other words, did you see your connection?
Recently, I happened to share with somebody an old poem I wrote many years ago.
It's a bit in the shade of Dong Po's Valley Sounds poem, in that the separation of self and environment becomes obscured and another, more intimate perspective emerges.
I won't say it's some kind of enlightenment poem, because unlike Dong Po, I did try to say something about it in the morning in this poem.
It was during the time I spent two years living in a tent in a traveling graduate school experience known then as the National Audubon Society Expedition Institute.
We had three-person A-frame tents.
The middle spot, squeezed between the two other people, was not favored by anyone, so I never had trouble claiming that spot.
But the middle of the A-frame gave me full sitting height, so I could get up a half hour before the wake-up call and meditate, wedged between my two tent partners.
This is where I developed what many of our Mountains and Rivers Retreat participants have come to know as the sleeping bag okesa, a way to wrap yourself in your sleeping bag for upright sitting.
We were in Florida, not in any sort of wilderness area that night, actually near a construction site.
Seemingly insentient objects populate the poem, even the dreaded machine by which humanity most egregiously manipulates the earth, the bulldozer.

What might not be obvious at first hearing is that I took all the words of the first stanza, which was written right then in the tent, and re-manipulated them later three more times into three more stanzas, using all the words.

The result was some sort of unpacking of frames of reference about identity, location, bodies, entities, and the whole somnambulant world of half-awareness we experience upon waking, when we habitually grasp back towards our grounding through a sense of me and other as a way to wake up.
This poem instead takes that fleeting personal disassociation and runs with it in the other direction, towards intimate connection, knowing and skinless openness.
Here's the poem, called "The Tent."
*In the dream morning I awaken to raven calls.
Outside the tent the bulldozers whine and rev.
Through the small opening of the flap I see transparent sky.
In that moment I don't know where I am.
The raven calls in the tent, whining through the opening.
My dream sees the morning as a small moment, transparent outside.
The bulldozers flap the sky and rev into an awakening, and I know I am not here.
The opening of the morning, flapping out through the tent, revolves and calls in the sky.
I know ravens and bulldozers, small and transparent, a whining in that moment of the dream awakens and I see that I am.
I don't know the transparent dream which I see through.
The raven, the bulldozer, the tent flap the morning past my small opening.
Outside I whine, I rev, I awaken in that moment where I am the sky calls.*
Yeah, this looks like the next page of my talk, completely disconnected from all other things, because it should be.
Because here Mountain Colours says:
*When you have true practice then valley sounds, colours, mountains, colours and sounds all reveal the 84,000 verses.
When you are free from fame, profit, body and mind, the valleys and mountains are also free.*
This is the end of the talk, but there's a part I want to put in here now.
It's about this idea of touching the other and having this transference and connection.
Laurie talks again in his book about Dongshan, who was the founder of our Soto school in China.
In China they called it the Caodong school, and this was the school that was then transmitted down through the centuries to Rujing, and that Dogen was transmitted to Dogen.
But it began with Dongshan, and Dongshan's innovation was a teaching he created called the five ranks.
I'll just read what Laurie says about this, because he describes it more succinctly and better than I could.
*One of Dongshan's great contributions is his formulation of a teaching called the five ranks, depicting the integration of dualities.
The first rank is the relative within the absolute.
This is emptiness, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body or mind, but there's no knowing it until we move to the next rank.
The second rank is the realization of that emptiness and it's referred to as the absolute within the relative.
So first we had the relative within the absolute and now we have the absolute within the relative.
This is where the enlightenment experience or Kensho happens, but still there is separation.
Absolute and relative are still dualistic.
So in this sense we often have had a notion about Kensho being some sort of ultimate experience.
Here Dongshan is saying it's simply a flipping of our normal viewpoint.
Rather than seeing the relative within the absolute, we see the absolute within relative.
We see things here in this relative world as being somehow absolute, eternal, imbued with some type of greatness beyond their mundane-ness and that's the Kensho experience essentially.
But he says it's still dualistic because there's still a separation between those two.*
*Now he spends some time talking about the third rank.
The third rank is coming from within the absolute.
When you realize the whole universe is nothing but yourself, you have to take care of it.
You have to be very selfish because that self is the 10,000 things existing in the past, present and future.
Every action you take affects the totality of that universe.
But understanding that doesn't impart much strength because in understanding there's still separation between the knower and the thing the knower knows.
Believing also doesn't impart strength.
A belief system is usually dependent on something else and thus is vulnerable.
But when you realize it, you transform your life and that transformation is empowering.
No longer in the abstract, the whole matter becomes your very life itself and inevitably compassion begins to happen.
You put your life on the line.
There's just no way to avoid it when you realize that in fact your life is already on the line.*
That is his comment on the third rank, of coming from within the absolute.
It sounds very much like an activist stance towards practice, but you're coming from a stance of the absolute: this is all of the great Dharma world that you're protecting.
Dongshan's fourth rank is arriving at mutual integration, the coming from both absolute and relative.
*At this stage, they still are two things like a mixture of salt and pepper.
There's integration, but in integration, there are still two things.
This is expressed with the image of the Bodhisattva whose face covered with dirt descends the mountain and re-enters the marketplace, like the end of the ten ox herding pictures.
In the fifth rank, unity attained, there is no longer a mixture.
It's one thing, neither absolute nor relative, up nor down, profane nor holy, good nor bad, male nor female.*
What is it?
And that "what is it" is sort of the driving question in the activism of your life.
So again, coming back to where I was before, Dogen wraps this up in the valley sounds, mountain colors fascicle.
At the end, he says:
*When you have true practice, then valley sounds and colors, mountain colors and sounds, all reveal the 84,000 verses.
When you're free from fame, profit, body, and mind, the valleys and mountains are also free.
Through the night, the valley sounds and mountain colors do and do not actualize the 84,000 verses.
When your capacity to talk about valleys and mountains as valleys and mountains is not yet mature, who can see and hear you as valley sounds and mountain colors?
Who can see and hear you as valley sounds and mountain colors?*
How can our activism have the weight of recognition?
How can others know that our expressions of concern for the planet should be listened to?

If they hear us as valley sounds and mountain colors, speaking with spiritual authority for the benefit of all beings, then our practice of intimacy with all things becomes in itself activism and advocacy.
Like Dr.
Seuss's Lorax, who springs up out of a freshly cut tree stump and says, "I speak for the trees": that is an authentic statement, for we will be of the trees and not apart from them.
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Well, thanks.
How are we doing on time?
Any questions or discussion, any comments people have?
Yeah, me too.
Yeah.
I'm going to have to listen back to my own talk, and maybe I'll find out what it was I was trying to say.
**Participant:** I like your [unclear: "full-genre"] references, the five ranks.
**Reizan Bob Penny:** The five ranks.
Yeah.
It's one of my favorite study projects.
**Participant:** Yeah.
It's something we should look into.
I think Dogen likes to mix it all up and controvert it and turn it around to trip our minds.
It's not like a systemized, progressive idea with Dogen going from one to two to three to four or something like that.
But the elements he's playing with are those relative and absolute and mixed in and out elements.
That's what Dogen is playing with in a lot of his writing, it seems like.
So he's sort of working with the five ranks, not referencing them exactly all the time, seems to me, or at least with the spirit of them.
Have you studied any books regarding Dongshan, Chris?
There is one.
This Is It.
It's called This Is It?
Yeah, I think so.
Oh, interesting.
It came out maybe four years ago.
Okay, so a fairly new book.
Yeah.
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Well, yeah, and he was a student of Nanquan at that period of time.
I don't recommend writing a poem like that.
Again, I doubt I'll write a poem again where I play with words like that.
It might feel like too much of a device, but in that case, it felt like it worked out and said something.
**Participant:** You know, I really appreciated the poetic work that you took into this tough, really tough matter that we're seeing out there, the climate.
And I'm always asking myself, what am I supposed to do?
What am I going to do here?
But sometimes I think just getting into that world of looking at it through that poetic lens just manifests itself.
It was the dream to come forward into action somehow.
And I was just kind of realizing as you were speaking, I don't have to struggle with that decision, because all these things in life are coming.
They're coming at me anyway, right?
I mean, there they are every day.
And so it's really very simple.
I can't sort of jump out of my boundary and need someplace else, because they're right here.
But I think that's what the poetry or Dogen's words, when we read Dogen's words, I think that's what they lend themselves to.
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Yeah, and we get infected by our typical political activist milieu, in which we understand how change happens.
We put upon ourselves the onus of responsibility that somehow we have to make a personal difference.
And somehow, if we do everything right, we'll fix the planet, but it's up to us.
And increasingly, it seems pretty clear that a lot of individuals are feeling like what I do personally isn't going to make a diddly bit of difference in the big picture.
This is too big, what's going on, which is true.
And so what do you do?
I think the main thing is that people need to care.
They need to care so deeply that they just can't allow it to happen.

And outside of that, outside of just caring and energizing your sense of care and connectedness to the mountains and the valleys and your deep spiritual identity with place, nothing's going to make a difference, really.
When great numbers of people care, it makes a difference.
That's what's going to make a difference.
And I think Greta Thunberg, for instance, has figured that out and talks about that.

That's what makes her so interesting as a personage in that activism world, somebody we can think about as maybe being almost a Dharmic teacher in a way, talking about life and death and existential realities.
Yeah.
Well, I suppose we can do our chants now.
Okay.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to amend them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
And I think we'll do refuges now.
